description: I´m Narek, economist and student of Mechatronics Engineering; I like challenges and hackatons.
summary: Earth data goes up and down all the time. To know if a change is a real trend, or only a season, El Niño or an error in one dataset, you need code and statistics that most students and local teams do not have. TrendSleuth is a free web app that does this work in seconds. You choose one of seven NASA variables (rain, temperature, hot days, cold nights, soil moisture, humidity or wind) and a 3D globe shows where a rise (green) or a fall (red) is confirmed. Then you choose any place on Earth. TrendSleuth reads up to 45 years of NASA data (MERRA-2, GPM IMERG and NASA POWER), removes the seasons and ten natural climate rhythms such as El Niño, tests what is left with the seasonal Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, and checks rain against a second NASA dataset. It answers the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant. The answer comes in three levels: Beginner (the verdict and a warning), Intermediate (the charts) and Pro (every test). Our goal is simple: help students, teachers and local decision makers tell a real change from a false alarm.
details:
1. The problem

Earth science data changes all the time. Rain, temperature or soil moisture can rise in one region and fall in another, even when the same process (for example El Niño) drives both. Seasons, natural climate rhythms and errors in a single dataset can look like a trend. To separate a real change from a false alarm you need many datasets, code and statistics. Most high-school and university students, teachers and local teams (water, energy, farming, local governments) do not have that time or training.

Our goal: a tool that anyone can use to select a variable, see how it changes over time, and know what is changing, where, how much, and if the change is significant.

2. What TrendSleuth does

Live app: https://kello69xddddd.github.io/trendsleuth/ (no login, works in any modern browser).

  • Step 1, choose a variable. Seven NASA variables with simple definitions: rain, temperature, hot days (daily maximum), cold nights (daily minimum), soil moisture, humidity and wind.
  • Global trend map. A 3D globe (NASA Blue Marble). Only confirmed trends are painted: green = rise, red = fall, stronger colour = faster change, no colour = not confirmed.
  • Step 2, choose a place. Search a country or province, type coordinates or tap the globe. The app names the province and country and downloads up to 45 years of monthly data from the NASA POWER API.
  • Step 3, read the result in three levels. Beginner: trend or no trend, a strength meter, the rate of change and one plain sentence, plus an outlook card (Warning / Watch / Low concern) with the change to 2050 if the trend continues and one adaptation action based on IPCC AR6. Intermediate: four interactive charts (over time, then vs now, natural rhythms, by month). Pro: every statistical test, all numbers, sources and downloads (JSON and CSV).
  • Top trends. For each variable, the region with the fastest confirmed rise and fall. One tap runs the full test there.
  • Learning tools. A guided demo that can be paused, nine solved case files and a glossary of 31 words with examples and units.

3. How it works (method)

  • Monthly anomalies remove the yearly cycle.
  • The engine tests ten repeating climate rhythms (El Niño 3.4, coastal El Niño 1+2, Indian Ocean Dipole, NAO, AO, PNA, Tropical North and South Atlantic, Southern Annular Mode, QBO) with a month-by-month regression and a lag of 0 to 6 months. The strongest rhythm is removed only if it is significant after a Bonferroni correction and explains at least 10% of the variation. The slow Pacific Decadal Oscillation is reported, not removed.
  • The trend is tested with the seasonal Mann-Kendall test (Hirsch-Slack correction), Sen's slope with a 95% confidence interval, and a t-test with AR(1)-adjusted errors.
  • Robustness checks: months with no active rhythm, the record without its last two years, and a second NASA dataset (rain must be confirmed by both MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG).
  • If there is no trend, the tool says how many years of data would be needed (Weatherhead et al., 1998).
  • The global map runs the same seasonal Mann-Kendall test on about 52,000 grid cells (1.0° x 1.25°, 1981-2025) with a 5% false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg).
  • The Python engine was validated against pymannkendall and synthetic data; the browser engine reproduces the Python results.

4. What we found (results)

  • Same El Niño, opposite results. Rain on Ecuador's coast follows the coastal El Niño index (37% of the monthly variation), while the Amazon basin of the Coca river responds in the opposite direction. There is no long-term rain trend there yet: it is a cycle.
  • A false lead. One NASA dataset alone shows a "highly significant" rain increase in the Coca basin (p = 0.0003). The second dataset does not confirm it. Over land, only 1 in 4 significant MERRA-2 rain trends is confirmed by IMERG.
  • A real trend. Quito warms by about +0.21 °C per decade (strong evidence).
  • A hidden trend. Over Nauru and the Gilbert Islands (Kiribati) the raw record shows no trend (p = 0.56). After removing El Niño, rain falls by about 15% per decade since 1998, and the second dataset agrees. We present it as a lead to check with rain gauges, not a final result.
  • Then vs now. On those islands the 2015-16 El Niño brought 113% more rain than normal; the 2026 El Niño, 72% so far.

5. Benefits and impact

TrendSleuth turns hours of data work into one clear and honest answer. Students learn how scientists decide if a change is significant. Teachers get ready-made cases. Local teams get a first warning to investigate. The tool also shows when a "trend" is a false alarm, which protects people from wrong decisions.

6. Creativity and design choices

  • A "detective" approach: every result is a verdict with evidence, not only a chart.
  • Two NASA datasets as two witnesses for rain.
  • One screen, no scroll, large text and three levels of depth, following WCAG 2.2 AA.
  • A global tool with a local story: El Niño in Ecuador.

7. Tools and technologies

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Numba, numcodecs, Matplotlib, pymannkendall for validation, pytest, Playwright), JavaScript, HTML and CSS, globe.gl and three.js, Plotly.js, mapshaper, GitHub and GitHub Pages. Code under the MIT license: https://github.com/kello69xddddd/trendsleuth

8. Limits and next steps

Straight-line trends only. A record of 28 to 46 years cannot fully separate a forced trend from slow natural variability. A link with a rhythm is an association, not proof of cause. Reanalysis data can contain artificial trends, so rain needs two sources for a strong verdict. The outlook is a sign to investigate, not a climate-model forecast. Next steps (proposal): a school pilot in December 2026, and a Spanish version with checks against weather stations in 2027.

9. Team

TRENDTRONIC, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Sangolquí (ESPE), Ecuador: Narek Vásconez (lead), Alejandro Benítez (frontend), Jorge Chapi (backend), Andrés Albán (visual design), Alexander Escobar (impact).

10. Use of artificial intelligence

We used Claude (Anthropic, models Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2) under the direction and review of the team for: research and reading the challenge resources, designing the method, writing and debugging the Python engine and the web app code, running the analysis on the NASA data, interface and pitch deck design, and writing and translating these texts. The team chose the challenge, the audience and the detective concept, wrote three lists of corrections during the event and reviewed every version and every result. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used: the figures are plots of NASA data and the globe is the NASA Blue Marble. No NASA logo or mark is used or modified. Full declaration, including work prepared before the official start: https://github.com/kello69xddddd/trendsleuth/blob/main/docs/AI_AND_PRIOR_WORK.md
